why_how.text: The manual opens with new rules, and two of them change what you do when a motorcycle pulls up beside you or a school bus flashes red.
Only one situation excuses you from a school bus stop, and confusing it with an ordinary two-way road is a costly error.

scenario.text: You are waiting at a red light when a motorcycle rolls up between your car and the next lane, and later a school bus ahead stops with red lights flashing but no stop arm out.

reasoning.text: The rider is lane sharing, which is legal, so you leave room; the bus lights are the trigger, so the folded arm does not matter.

result.text: You hold your lane for the rider and stop at least twenty feet behind the bus.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking you may drive past a school bus with flashing red lights because its stop arm is still folded.

correction.text: The flashing red lights alone require the stop, at least twenty feet back, whatever the stop arm is doing.

memory_support.text: Riders may split, so make room; red lights flash, so stop twenty feet back.

prompt.text: On an undivided road, does a driver coming toward a stopped school bus with flashing red lights have to stop?

answer.text: Yes; only drivers going the opposite way on a divided highway are excused.

rationale.text: Without a divider, traffic in both directions stops for the flashing red lights.

title.text: New rules for sharing the road

lines.text: School bus red lights mean stop

narration.text: This first unit covers two rules that the manual places at the very front because they are new or often misunderstood. The first is about motorcycles. In Minnesota a rider may now travel or pass in the space between your vehicle and a vehicle in the next lane. The second is about school buses with flashing red lights, which tell you that children are getting on or off. By the end of this unit you will know how to treat a rider who moves up beside you, how far back to stop for a bus, why the stop arm is not the signal that matters, and the one situation in which you are allowed to keep going.

lines.text: Lane sharing is legal in Minnesota

narration.text: Lane sharing means a motorcycle rides or passes in the gap between two vehicles, or uses part of your lane. You will most often see it at a stoplight, as riders move forward to the front of the line, but a rider may also pass slow traffic on your left or on your right. Because this is legal, the rider is not doing anything wrong, and your job is simple. Do not drift over to close the gap, do not speed up to keep the rider behind you, and do not interfere with the motorcycle's safe movement. Treat the rider as a lawful road user who needs a little space to get by.

title.text: When a school bus flashes red

lines.text: Red lights mean students boarding or leaving
Stop no closer than twenty feet

narration.text: Flashing red lights on a school bus mean students are boarding or leaving the bus. When you see them on a stopped bus, you must bring your vehicle to a stop, and you must stop no closer than twenty feet from the bus. That distance is the minimum, so stopping farther back is always allowed. Remember that the red lights are a command, not a suggestion. Slowing down and creeping past is not enough. You stay stopped while the red lights are flashing, and you keep that twenty-foot cushion between your front bumper and the bus the whole time.

lines.text: The stop arm is not the trigger
Red lights alone require a stop

narration.text: Here is a trap many new drivers fall into. They watch for the stop arm, the small sign that swings out from the side of the bus, and they assume that if the arm stays folded they may keep driving. The manual is clear that this is wrong. You must stop for a school bus showing flashing red lights even when its stop arm has not swung out. The flashing red lights are the trigger, so a bus whose arm stays folded still requires you to stop at least twenty feet away. If you ever see red lights flashing on a bus, stop first and look for the arm second, never the other way around.

lines.text: One exception: divided highway, opposite direction
Undivided road means both directions stop

narration.text: There is exactly one exception to stopping for a school bus with flashing red lights. If you are on a divided highway and traveling in the opposite direction from the bus, you are not required to stop. Everyone else stops. That includes drivers behind the bus and drivers beside it. On an undivided road, even one with several lanes, drivers going the opposite way must stop too, because nothing separates them from children crossing. Failing to stop is serious, and it can bring fines and a suspension of your driver's license, so when in doubt about whether a road counts as divided, stop.

lines.text: Undivided road, oncoming bus flashing red

narration.text: Here is a quick check: you are driving on an undivided two-way road and a school bus coming toward you stops with its red lights flashing. Do you have to stop? Think it through using the exception you just learned. The only drivers excused are those going the opposite way on a divided highway. This road has no divider. So the answer is yes, you must stop, just like the drivers behind the bus. Traffic in both directions stops on an undivided road, and you stay at least twenty feet back until the red lights stop flashing. If you got that right, you have the most tested school bus rule down.

lines.text: Red lights: stop twenty feet back
Only divided highway, opposite way, is excused

narration.text: Let us wrap up this unit. A motorcycle may legally ride or pass between lanes, most often at a stoplight, and your duty is to leave it room rather than block it. Flashing red lights on a school bus mean students are boarding or leaving, and you must stop no closer than twenty feet from the bus. The stop arm does not decide anything; the red lights do. The single exception is a divided highway when you are going the opposite way. Skipping a school bus stop can cost you fines and a suspended license. Next you will look at work zones, office conduct and the online tools that save time.

why_how.text: Work zones put people inches from traffic, and the DVS office rules and online tools decide how smoothly your own licensing visit goes.

scenario.text: Sam plans a DVS visit in six weeks and starts the online pre-application today to get it out of the way.

reasoning.text: The pre-application should be started no more than thirty days before the visit, so starting six weeks early falls outside the window.

result.text: Sam waits until the visit is within thirty days, finishes the pre-application, and brings the confirmation page with every listed document.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking the thirty-day pre-application window is the same as a permit holding period.

correction.text: The thirty days only governs when you start the online pre-application before an office visit; it has nothing to do with how long you hold a permit.

memory_support.text: Watch the crews, respect the staff, and pre-apply within thirty days.

prompt.text: What happens to a customer who uses abusive language and refuses staff instructions at a DVS office?

answer.text: The customer is asked to leave and police are called.

rationale.text: DVS does not tolerate disruptive, abusive or violent conduct, and interfering with staff is also a crime.

narration.text: This unit gathers several reminders from the front of the manual. First comes work zone safety, because crews work very close to moving traffic and the vehicles around them can behave unpredictably. Then you will see the conduct rules that apply in Driver and Vehicle Services offices and the law that protects the people who work there. After that comes the Commissioner's message about what it means to hold a license. Finally, you will learn how the online pre-application, its thirty-day timing and the DVS virtual assistant can make your visit faster and help you keep track of your records.

In a work zone you need to stay alert for three things that the manual names together: distracted driving, zipper merges and lane patterns that have been changed. The reason is simple and serious. Road crews work very close to moving traffic, and large construction vehicles can move in ways you do not expect. A driver who glances at a phone, misses a merge point or follows old lane lines can end up in a space where workers are standing. Put the phone away, follow the signs and markings for the new lane layout, and take your turn at the merge point when lanes come together.

lines.text: Interfering with staff is a crime
Abuse or violence: asked to leave

narration.text: Driver and Vehicle Services sets clear rules for how customers behave. It does not tolerate disruptive behavior, harassment, obscene or abusive language or gestures, interfering with services, refusing staff instructions, or violent conduct. A customer who does any of these is asked to leave, and police are called. Interfering with or obstructing the work of a DVS employee is also a crime under a Minnesota statute, and the manual names both acts under the same law. These rules protect the staff and every other customer waiting in line, so keep calm, follow instructions and ask questions politely.

The Commissioner's message in the manual gives the reason behind all of these rules. Driving is a privilege, and it carries a responsibility to everyone else on the road. The message names three habits that show you take that responsibility seriously: buckle up every time, obey speed laws, and never drive under the influence of alcohol. Keep those three in mind as you study the rest of the manual, because many of the later chapters, from seat belts to speed limits to impaired driving, are simply the details of how to keep this promise to other people sharing the road.

lines.text: Start within thirty days of visiting

narration.text: Before you visit a DVS office, you can use the pre-application in DVS online services. It lets you complete a large part of your license application ahead of time and shows which documents each license type requires, which shortens your time at the counter. Start it no more than thirty days before your office visit so you do not have to fill out a paper application, and bring the confirmation page along with every document it lists. For questions, the virtual assistant at drive.mn.gov answers in English, Spanish, Somali and Hmong, and a MyDVS account lets you follow your license and registration information online.

title.text: Thirty days is not permit time

lines.text: Thirty days: when to start pre-application
Permit holding is a different rule

narration.text: Watch out for a number that is easy to mix up. The thirty-day window you just learned governs when you start the online pre-application before an office visit. Staying inside that window is what lets you skip a paper application. It is not a permit holding period, and it does not tell you how long you must have a permit before a road test. Those holding times are measured in months and depend on your age, and you will meet them later in this chapter. If a question mentions thirty days, ask yourself whether it is about paperwork timing or about driving experience before you choose an answer.

Here is a quick check: a customer at a DVS office starts using abusive language and refuses to follow staff instructions. What happens next? Think back to the conduct rules. Driver and Vehicle Services does not tolerate disruptive or abusive behavior or refusing staff instructions, and a customer who does these things is asked to leave while police are called. Remember too that interfering with or obstructing a DVS employee's work is a crime under Minnesota law. The safest choice for everyone, including you, is to stay calm, follow directions and ask for help in a respectful way if something is unclear.

To recap, work zones call for full attention to distracted driving, zipper merges and changed lanes, because crews are close and machines move unpredictably. In DVS offices, abusive or disruptive conduct gets a customer asked to leave with police called, and interfering with or obstructing staff is a crime. The Commissioner reminds you that driving is a privilege with real responsibilities. Before any visit, start the online pre-application within thirty days and bring the confirmation page and listed documents, and use the virtual assistant or a MyDVS account when you need help. Next, you will prepare for the written test.

title.text: Getting ready for the written test

why_how.text: The written test checklist tells you exactly what to bring, and teens have extra documents and an age minimum to meet.

scenario.text: Maya is fifteen, has finished classroom instruction and has behind-the-wheel lessons scheduled, and she wants to take the written test next week.

reasoning.text: She meets the age minimum, and a finished classroom course with lessons scheduled is what the Blue Card shows.

result.text: Maya books the test, finishes the pre-application within thirty days, brings her Blue Card, identification and fee money, and has a parent sign her application.

claim.text: Common mistake: assuming the minimum teen age for the written test is the same as the road test age.

correction.text: A teen may take the written test at fifteen, which is a different age from the road test minimum.

memory_support.text: Fifteen for the written test, Blue if finished, Pink if partway.

prompt.text: A teen is enrolled in a concurrent driver education course and has finished the first fifteen classroom hours. Which card shows this?

rationale.text: The Pink Card shows enrollment in a concurrent course with the first fifteen classroom hours done, while the Blue Card shows classroom work is finished.

narration.text: The written test is your first step toward a Minnesota license, and the manual gives you a checklist so nothing is forgotten on the day. In this unit you will go through it item by item. Everyone needs a scheduled appointment, a completed online pre-application, identification and money for fees. Applicants under eighteen have more to think about: a minimum age, a card that shows where they are in driver education, and an application signed by the right adult. Getting these details right means you will not be turned away before you even sit down to answer questions.

lines.text: Bring ID, fee money, Social Security number

narration.text: Start with the basics. Before the Class D written test you need a scheduled test appointment. The checklist tells you to finish the online pre-application at the DPS MyDVS site within the thirty days before that appointment, and not earlier. On the day itself, bring the identification the checklist requires and money to pay the fees. You should also know your Social Security number if you are eligible to have one. None of this is difficult, but missing a single item can mean rescheduling, so lay everything out the night before and check it against the list.

lines.text: Fifteen is the minimum teen age

narration.text: If you are under eighteen, you must be at least fifteen years old to take the written test. You also bring one of two cards. The Blue Card shows that classroom instruction is finished and behind-the-wheel training is scheduled. The Pink Card shows that you are enrolled in a concurrent driver education course and have completed the first fifteen classroom hours. Your application must be signed and approved by a parent, a court-appointed guardian, a county-appointed foster parent, or the director of the transitional living program where you live, with documentation if the signer is not a parent, and you bring the Supplemental Parental Curriculum certificate.

Here is a common slip. Because the written test and the road test appear on the same checklist pages, some teens assume they share one minimum age. They do not. A teen must be at least fifteen to take the written test, and that is a different age from the road test minimum you will see on the next checklist page. Keep the two apart in your mind by linking each age to its own card. The written test goes with the Blue or Pink Card that shows your driver education is under way, and the road test comes later, with a different card and a higher age.

Here is a quick check: a teen is enrolled in a concurrent driver education course and has finished the first fifteen classroom hours. Which card shows this for the written test? Think about what each card means. The Blue Card is for a teen whose classroom instruction is complete and whose behind-the-wheel lessons are scheduled. The Pink Card is for a teen who is still enrolled in a concurrent course but has completed the first fifteen classroom hours. So the answer is the Pink Card. Either card admits a teen to the written test, as long as the age and signature rules are also met.

lines.text: Teens: fifteen, Blue or Pink Card

narration.text: To sum up, every written test applicant needs a scheduled appointment, an online pre-application finished within the thirty days before it, the required identification, money for fees and knowledge of their Social Security number if they are eligible for one. Teens must be at least fifteen, bring either the Blue Card or the Pink Card, and have an application signed and approved by a parent or one of the other listed adults, plus the Supplemental Parental Curriculum certificate. With this list complete, you are ready to sit the test. The next unit moves on to what you need on road test day.

why_how.text: On road test day the examiner checks you, your permit, your licensed companion and the car itself, and any gap can cancel the test.

scenario.text: Leo arrives for his road test with his permit and a car whose brake lights and turn signals work and whose registration is current, but he drove himself and has no licensed driver along.

reasoning.text: The checklist requires a licensed driver to come with the applicant, and without one the road test may be cancelled.

result.text: Leo reschedules and returns with a licensed driver, hands his permit to the examiner and shows insurance proof on his phone.

claim.text: Common mistake: believing only a paper insurance card is accepted at the road test.

correction.text: Electronic proof from the insurer's website or shown on a device is accepted, along with the original card or the declaration page.

memory_support.text: Licensed driver along, permit to examiner, safe car, proof of insurance.

prompt.text: A road test car has current registration and working lights, but its rear door will not open from the inside. Is it ready for the test?

answer.text: No, doors must open from both inside and outside.

rationale.text: The road test vehicle must be safe, including doors that open from inside and outside, working seat belts and working lights.

narration.text: Road test day is when everything you have practiced comes together, but the test can end before it starts if the paperwork or the car is not ready. In this unit you will learn the checklist the manual gives every road test applicant. It covers what you need to schedule and complete online, the person who must come with you, the permit you hand over, the condition and registration of the vehicle, and the forms of insurance proof the examiner will accept. Treat it like a preflight checklist. Go through each line before you leave home, and the examiner can focus on your driving.

For the road test you need an appointment and a completed online pre-application, just as you did for the written test. The new item is a person. You must bring a licensed driver who comes with you to the test, and without that licensed driver the road test may be cancelled. When the test begins, you hand your valid instruction permit to the examiner. Plan ahead for who will come along, because the appointment time is fixed and a missing companion is one of the easiest ways to lose your slot. Confirm with that person ahead of time that they hold a valid license and can be there.

The vehicle you bring must be safe. Its doors must open from both inside and outside, the seat belts must work, and the headlights, taillights, brake lights and turn signals must all function. The registration must be current or covered by a sixty-day permit. Before the test, have someone stand outside the car while you press the brake and switch on each signal, and try every door handle from both sides. Fixing a burned-out bulb the day before is far easier than finding the problem at the test site in front of the examiner.

Many applicants worry that they must find a paper insurance card. The manual lists three accepted forms of proof for the road test vehicle. You may show the original card from the insurance company, the policy declaration page, or electronic proof, either from the insurer's website or shown on a device. That means a clear image of your proof on your phone is fine. What matters is that the proof is from the insurer and covers the vehicle you bring. Make sure your phone is charged and the proof loads before you arrive, so you are not searching for a signal while the examiner waits.

lines.text: Rear door will not open inside

narration.text: Here is a quick check: the car you plan to use has current registration and every light works, but one rear door will not open from the inside. Is it ready for the road test? Think about the vehicle checklist. The road test vehicle must be safe, and that includes doors that open from both inside and outside, working seat belts and working lights. A door that only opens from the outside fails that check, so the car is not ready. Get the door repaired or bring a different vehicle that meets every item, and confirm the registration and insurance proof for that vehicle too.

Here is the road test day list in one place. Bring your appointment, your completed online pre-application and a licensed driver who comes with you, because without that driver the test may be cancelled. Hand your valid instruction permit to the examiner. Bring a safe vehicle whose doors open inside and out, whose belts and lights all work, and whose registration is current or covered by a sixty-day permit. Show insurance proof as the original card, the declaration page or electronic proof on a device. Next, you will see the age and permit time rules that decide when you may take the road test.

why_how.text: The age you are when you apply decides how long you must hold a permit and what documents prove you are ready for the road test.
Teens carry the heaviest checklist, so knowing it early prevents a wasted trip.

scenario.text: Ava is sixteen, has held her permit for six months without any convictions, and did two of those months while living in another state.

reasoning.text: Teens need six clean months, and driving done in another state counts if a certified record from that state is brought.

result.text: Ava brings her White Card, her signed Supervised Driving Log, the parental approval on her application and a certified record from the other state.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking every adult needs only three months of permit holding before the road test.

correction.text: Eighteen-year-olds still need six months; only applicants aged nineteen or older drop to three months.

memory_support.text: Under nineteen holds six months, nineteen and up holds three.

prompt.text: An applicant aged nineteen has held a permit for four months. Has the permit holding requirement been met?

answer.text: Yes; applicants aged nineteen or older need at least three months.

rationale.text: Six months applies to teens and eighteen-year-olds, while three months applies from age nineteen.

narration.text: Before you can book a road test, you have to meet the rules for your age group. This unit compares them. Teens under eighteen have the most requirements: a minimum age, a certificate of completed driver education, a clean permit record over a set period, and a signed record of supervised practice. Applicants who are eighteen and applicants who are nineteen or older have simpler rules, but their permit holding times are not the same. By the end you should be able to hear an applicant's age and permit history and say whether they are ready for the road test.

A road test applicant under eighteen must be at least sixteen years old. The teen also brings the White Card, which shows that driver education has been completed. This is different from the cards used for the written test. The Blue and Pink Cards show that driver education is finished in the classroom or still under way, and they admit a teen to the written test. The White Card certifies the whole course is done and belongs to the road test. If you mix them up and bring a Pink Card on road test day, you will not be able to test.

lines.text: Permit held for the past six months

narration.text: A teen must have held an instruction permit for the past six months before the road test. Those months must also be clean: no conviction for a moving violation, and no conviction for an alcohol or controlled substance violation. This condition is spelled out for teens, and the adult lines of the checklist do not repeat it. In practice, a single moving violation conviction during those six months means the teen is not yet eligible. Drive carefully during your permit months, because they are not only practice time but also part of what qualifies you to test.

Some families move during the permit period. If some or all of a teen's six months of permit driving took place in another state, the teen brings a certified driving record from that state. That record shows the months were held and supports eligibility for the provisional license. The record must be certified, so an ordinary printout or a letter will not do. Along with it, the teen brings a Supervised Driving Log that is filled in and signed by a parent or guardian, plus the parental approval signature on the application. These documents together show both the time and the supervised practice behind it.

lines.text: Nineteen or older: at least three months

narration.text: The permit holding rule also applies to adults, but it splits at age nineteen. An applicant who is eighteen must have held the instruction permit for at least six months, the same length as teens. An applicant who is nineteen or older needs at least three months. So the six-month rule covers everyone under nineteen, and only from age nineteen does the requirement drop to three months. When you read a question about permit time, check the age first. Eighteen and nineteen sound close, but they sit on opposite sides of this line.

title.text: Not every adult gets three months

narration.text: Here is the trap. Because eighteen is the age of adulthood, many people assume an eighteen-year-old gets the shorter adult holding time. The manual does not work that way. Permit holding time before the road test is six months for applicants under eighteen and for eighteen-year-olds, and only three months for applicants aged nineteen or older. An eighteen-year-old who has held a permit for four months is not yet eligible, while a nineteen-year-old with the same four months is. Keep the dividing line at nineteen, not eighteen, and this question becomes easy.

lines.text: Age nineteen, permit held four months

narration.text: Here is a quick check: an applicant who is nineteen years old has held an instruction permit for four months. Has the permit holding requirement for the road test been met? Use the dividing line you just learned. Six months applies to teens and to eighteen-year-olds, and three months applies to applicants aged nineteen or older. This applicant is nineteen, so the minimum is three months, and four months is enough. The answer is yes. If the same applicant were eighteen, four months would fall short, because an eighteen-year-old needs at least six months of permit holding.

lines.text: Teens: sixteen, White Card, six clean months

narration.text: To finish, here are the road test eligibility rules by age. Teens must be at least sixteen, bring the White Card, and have held a permit for the past six months with no moving, alcohol or controlled substance convictions. Months driven in another state count if the teen brings a certified driving record from that state, and every teen brings a signed Supervised Driving Log and the parental approval on the application. Eighteen-year-olds need six months of permit holding, and applicants nineteen or older need three. With these rules and the earlier checklists, you are ready to plan both of your tests.
